summary: Introductory discovery to understand Novus Ventures' inference cost constraints. Discussed per-token economics, batching and caching levers, hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs, security requirements (SOC2, KMS), and pilot next steps. Customer is cost-sensitive with strict latency SLO for customer-facing features. Agreed to run pilot and exchange detailed pricing and benchmark artifacts.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-06-01
Start: 14:30 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Kelly Monroe (Redwood AE), Diego Ramirez (Redwood SE), Lina Park (Redwood Solutions), Anika Shah (Novus Head of ML), Marcus Lee (Novus VP Eng), Priya Patel (Novus SRE), Sanjay Rao (Novus Security)

Auto-summary (auto): Discussion focused on cost composition and choosing hosting mode for a customer-facing recommendation feature.

00:00:05 Kelly Monroe: hey everyone thanks for joining im kelly from redwood, um quick round robin before we jump in, can folks say name and role?
00:00:12 Anika Shah: hi im anika head of ml here at novus, i own model selection and evaluation
00:00:16 Marcus Lee: marcus here, vp eng, long-term owner of infra decisions
00:00:20 Priya Patel: priya, sres, i'll be owning the rollout and observability side
00:00:24 Sanjay Rao: sanjay, security, i'll be validating compliance needs
00:00:28 Kelly Monroe: awesome thanks. diego where you want to kick off?
00:00:32 Diego Ramirez: yeah thanks kelly. quick agenda: we want to understand your usage profile, latency targets, data residency/compliance constraints, and cost ceiling so we can map hosted/dedicated/private options and batching/cache levers to unit economics. sound good?
00:00:46 Anika Shah: yes thats exactly it. to give context, we have a recommender used in our mobile app, about 150k monthly active users, peak concurrency about 450 reqs per minute, average prompt length about 140 tokens in and ~60 tokens out. latency target is median <= 300ms end-to-end for the recommendation API. cost target is tight: we cant exceed $0.0025 per inference on average right now.
00:01:10 Marcus Lee: and we are sensitive to data - some PII flows in the events, so if hosted, we need strong contract protections and KMS/HSM for keys, otherwise we'll look at VPC/private.
00:01:20 Diego Ramirez: great, a couple quick clarifying q's: is the 300ms from when the mobile client hits your edge or from your API gateway? and is the 0.0025 number steadystate or initial pilot?
00:01:30 Anika Shah: 300ms is from our gateway to client — so that includes network hop into model. The 0.0025 is what finance has targeted steady-state; pilot can be higher but they'd like an expected path to that number.
00:01:42 Diego Ramirez: got it. so couple pieces to map: model size/architecture, tokens per request, and the ratio of cold vs hot requests — that drives batching opportunities and KV cache hit rate. can you share model family? are you using open LLMs or a proprietary encoder?
00:01:58 Anika Shah: right now a tuned open-architecture encoder-decoder -- think ~7B-ish with a few adapters, not heavy fine-tuning. we can experiment with smaller variants if needed.
00:02:07 Kelly Monroe: okay good, thats typical. two big levers to get to unit targets: batching (amortize per-request overhead) and kv/prefix caching (avoid recomputing encoder work). we'll also talk about quantization, which changes throughput and quality tradeoffs.
00:02:20 Marcus Lee: how predictable is batching with mobile traffic? some of our traffic is spikey — mornings have a big spike.
00:02:27 Diego Ramirez: great question. redwood supports continuous batching with adaptive windows: small windows for latency-sensitive traffic and longer windows when the system can tolerate slightly higher p99. that means the hosted offering can still keep median low while improving throughput at peaks. however, batching alone won't meet your $0.0025 target if every request is independent compute. where caching helps is when you have repeated prefixes — for recommenders we often see repeat contexts across sessions so prefix or KV cache hit can reduce decoder work substantially.
00:02:58 Priya Patel: whats typical cache hit rate in your customer benchmarks?
00:03:01 Diego Ramirez: varies but for e-comm recommender workloads i've seen 25-40% hit rates early, sometimes up to 60% with good normalization and prompt templating. we also offer heuristic suggestions for deduping prefixes to improve hits.
00:03:15 Anika Shah: hmm we do have a lot of templated prompts so 30-35% seems realistic. what about quantization impacts on quality? we cant drop below a certain accuracy for recommendations.
00:03:27 Diego Ramirez: right — quantization to int8 or 4-bit can cut per-token cost 20-40% depending on kernel and model shape. quality regression is model-dependent; we recommend A/B evals and redwood optimize will suggest safe profiles. for your use case i'd recommend testing int8 first and validate against your rec-sim metrics.
00:03:45 Kelly Monroe: to map to dollars, we usually build a per-token cost model: base compute cost (per-VPU-hour or per-GPU-hour amortized), memory footprint affecting slot density, plus network and storage. for hosted we present a per-token price that bundles compute and caching layer. for dedicated/private we provide committed capacity pricing with effective per-token calculations depending on utilization.
00:04:08 Marcus Lee: can you give a ballpark split? like what percent of cost is compute vs memory vs overhead?
00:04:14 Diego Ramirez: ballpark for a mid-size model: compute about 65-75% of token cost, memory and idle footprint 10-20%, network and storage ~5-10%. but that shifts a lot with batching and cache: if cache hit increases from 0 to 30% you could see effective per-token compute drop by roughly 25-30% because you're avoiding decoder or encoder recompute.
00:04:36 Anika Shah: okay that helps. on the hosted contract: will hosted give us KMS integration? we need to manage keys centrally.
00:04:44 Kelly Monroe: yes hosted can integrate with customer-managed keys for data at rest and we have contractual controls and SOC2 artifacts; for absolute control customers choose Dedicated with a VPC peering or Private deployment if they need on-prem or air-gapped and their own KMS/HSM. sanjay do you have a must-have checklist?
00:04:58 Sanjay Rao: mostly SOC2, audit logs for token-level requests, SSO/SAML support, and an ability to attest key management. also we want proof of zero-persistence for ephemeral data in the pipeline.
00:05:10 Lina Park: we can share our compliance binder with SOC2 Type II report and a whitepaper on key handling. we also have an audit-log export feature that streams model call metadata into your SIEM.
00:05:21 Sanjay Rao: ok good.
00:05:24 Priya Patel: for dedicated or private, whats the ops burden? we cant staff a big team for model ops.
00:05:30 Diego Ramirez: Dedicated is managed by redwood, we operate the runtime but it's reserved capacity for you — autoscaling policies are configurable and we can enable on-call handoffs. Private is more hands-on: if you pick our VPC private control plane we still manage the control plane but compute can be customer-provisioned or we can provide an on-prem package; that has more integration work.
00:05:49 Marcus Lee: for our volumes, would you recommend starting hosted then move to dedicated? or start dedicated?
00:05:55 Kelly Monroe: depends on tolerance for variability. many customers start hosted to move faster, run a 4-8 week pilot, and then evaluate dedicated if their steady-state utilization and latency SLAs justify reserved capacity. given your $0.0025 steady state target, we'll run some scenarios — sometimes dedicated gets cheaper at 40-60% sustained utilization depending on model and kernel efficiency.
00:06:17 Anika Shah: can we see an example scenario? like if we have 450 rpm concurrency peaks and average token counts as i said, what does hosted per-inference look like vs dedicated?
00:06:26 Diego Ramirez: i'll put numbers in the spreadsheet but quick rough: hosted per-inf might be $0.0035-$0.005 for a 7B model without cache; with 30% cache and moderate batching you might hit $0.002-$0.003 hosted. Dedicated, amortizing GPU cost, could be $0.0012-$0.0025 depending on utilization and whether you can use quantized kernels. again these are rough.
00:06:50 Marcus Lee: that's promising. what about fallback and graceful degradation — if dedicated saturates do you have auto-fallback to hosted?
00:06:57 Kelly Monroe: yes, smart routing allows fallbacks by policy: we can route overflow to hosted or to smaller model variants. you can set cost-priority, latency-priority, or region-priority fallback rules.
00:07:08 Anika Shah: ok good. another practical question: how do you measure per-token in complex flows? we have pre and post processing outside the model that sometimes inflates token counts, and we do RAG calls as well.
00:07:19 Diego Ramirez: we instrument at the token level in the runtime — we capture model tokens consumed and provide token-level cost breakdown. for RAG flows you can choose where to run retrieval and how to slice the docs; those are additional tokens. we can help model your end-to-end token usage with a small tracing probe.
00:07:34 Priya Patel: about benchmarks, what do you need from us to run a representative pilot?
00:07:38 Diego Ramirez: ideal: a small prompt corpus of 200-500 representative requests, target latency SLOs, and a traffic pattern sample for 24 hours. we'll run latency+throughput tests against hosted and a dedicated-equivalent config. i'll send a template.
00:07:51 Anika Shah: we can get that. finance will also want sensitivity analysis: if cache hit drops to 10% what happens to cost? if we enable quantization what's the quality hit? can you model that?
00:08:03 Kelly Monroe: yes we'll include sensitivity cells in the spreadsheet: cache hit scenarios (10/30/50%), batching window sizes, model quantization levels, and expected per-token outcomes. we'll also show a path to reach your $0.0025 steady-state.
00:08:15 Marcus Lee: curious on multi-region: we need EU residency for some customers. does hosted support region pinning?
00:08:21 Lina Park: yes hosted supports region-specific deployment and data residency; we also support private deployments in EU if reqd.
00:08:27 Sanjay Rao: whats the SLA on hosted?
00:08:29 Kelly Monroe: we have SLA options for enterprise customers; hosted comes with standard uptime and 99.9% for paid tiers, dedicated gets stronger contractual guarantees. we'll attach the SLA matrix.
00:08:39 Anika Shah: how do you handle model versioning and rollbacks during canary? we cant risk corruption of user experience.
00:08:46 Diego Ramirez: redwood console supports model version pins, A/B rollouts, and automatic fallback if error rates spike. you can set thresholds on latency and correctness signals and automatically roll back.
00:08:55 Priya Patel: ok thats useful. last thing for now: billing cycle and commitment — finance wants to understand the minimum to make dedicated worthwhile.
00:09:03 Kelly Monroe: dedicated is monthly or annual commit. typically to be cheaper than hosted you'd need 40-60% sustained GPU utilization. we'll model sample commit sizes in the spreadsheet.
00:09:13 Marcus Lee: great. any immediate blockers from our side to start the pilot?
00:09:17 Anika Shah: we'll need to confirm a small budget and give you the prompt corpus; also need security to sign an NDA or data processing appendix for hosted tests.
00:09:26 Sanjay Rao: yes send DPA and our vendor assessment checklist.
00:09:29 Kelly Monroe: we'll send both.
00:09:31 Diego Ramirez: action-wise: i'll put together the benchmark template and a quick script that simulates your token distributions; kelly will send pricing scenarios + sensitivity spreadsheet; lina will attach SOC2 and KMS docs. can we reconvene for a pilot scoping on tuesday 6/8?
00:09:47 Priya Patel: tuesday works for me in the morning pst.
00:09:50 Anika Shah: works for me too.
:09:52 Kelly Monroe: perfect, well leave it there. thanks everyone.

Post-meeting notes (auto):
- Redwood to deliver pilot pricing spreadsheet with hosted/dedicated/private scenarios and sensitivity cells for cache hit, batching, and quantization.
- SE to provide benchmark script and prompt corpus template.
- Security to receive SOC2 and KMS integration docs; customer to send vendor checklist.
- Schedule pilot scoping 2027-06-08 morning PST.
